title: Juan Diego, saint (2002)
hookLine: the Indigenous visionary of Guadalupe canonized almost five centuries later

cards: Early one morning, a man named Juan Diego is walking past a hill called Tepeyac, on his way to Mass. He hears singing, like birds, coming from the top.
Then a woman's voice calls him by name, tenderly, in his own language, Nahuatl. He climbs, and finds a lady standing there, her clothes shining like the sun.
The account of what follows is called the Nican Mopohua, from its opening words in Nahuatl.

teach.b: In the account, the lady says she is the Virgin Mary, and asks for a church on that spot, where she can show her love to all who come. She sends Juan Diego to the bishop in the city to ask for it.
The bishop listens politely and sends him away.
Juan Diego goes back up the hill and begs her to send someone important instead. He calls himself a little man, a nobody, a tail, a leaf, someone others carry.
She answers that she has plenty of messengers, and she chooses him. Then, the sign. The bishop asks for proof.
On the hilltop, in the cold season, Juan Diego finds flowers blooming, gathers them into his tilma, the rough cloak he wears, and carries them to the bishop.
When he opens the cloak, the flowers fall out, and on the cloth is an image of the lady. That cloak hangs in the basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

teach.h: HER NAME FOR HIM: THE YOUNGEST.
teach.b: Again and again in the account, Mary calls him by tender words for the smallest, youngest child in a family. A line in Matthew's Gospel fits him.
In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus thanks his Father, "because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones."
Pope John Paul the Second declared Juan Diego a saint at that same basilica. The man who asked to be replaced by someone important became the one remembered.

how: Catholics keep Saint Juan Diego's feast in December, just before the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe; pilgrims come to the basilica in Mexico City to see the tilma, and parishes across the Americas celebrate Guadalupe with Masses, processions and roses.

o: a Spanish friar who first preached in Nahuatl
the bishop of Mexico who built a church on Tepeyac
the Indigenous man who carried flowers to a doubting bishop

games.q: the little one — tap the pairs.
p: his rough cloak, full of flowers
the account, named for its first words

s: Juan Diego asked Mary to send someone more important
he called himself a nobody; she chose him anyway.
the bishop believed him the first time
the bishop sent him away, and later asked for a sign.
in the account, Mary speaks to him in Nahuatl
she calls him by name, tenderly, in his own language.

games.q: you're Juan Diego. the bishop doubts you, and you think you're a nobody. the lady on the hill asks you to go back. what do you say?
o: please send someone important; they'll be believed.
I'll go, and I won't say a word about myself.
games.why: he begs her to send someone of standing. she answers that she has many messengers, and she chooses him.

practice: Picture Juan Diego on the road with his cloak bundled in his arms, walking toward a bishop who doubted him, and stay with him a while.

If you pray, ask for his prayers, or for the prayers of another Indigenous saint you know, such as Kateri Tekakwitha. If you don't, simply honor him in the quiet: a man who thought he was too small, and went anyway.

wordCard.voice: Juan Diego. The Indigenous man who, in the account of Guadalupe, carried flowers in his cloak to a doubting bishop, and was named a saint at the basilica beside that hill. Today's word.

orig.note: Nahuatl, written in Latin letters: my youngest one, as Mary calls Juan Diego in the Nican Mopohua.

carryVoice: Your line: the little one. Prayer in paint, a church that has sinned, two hands almost touching, honest memory, a man who changed, people truly human, and now the little one. Day eight hundred forty, done.
